papers.title: Actuator Reality Shaping for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Robot Learning
papers.abstract: Sim-to-real transfer in robot learning is often limited by discrepancies between the ideal actuator dynamics assumed during policy training and the nonlinear, hardware-dependent behavior of physical motors. While conventional approaches attempt to bridge this gap by increasing simulator fidelity through system identification, domain randomization, or learned actuator models, we introduce an alternative paradigm: actuator reality shaping. Instead of modifying the simulator to match the real world, our method shapes the closed-loop behavior of physical actuators to match the idealized second-order reference dynamics used in simulation. By equipping each joint with a two-degree-of-freedom feedforward--feedback controller, we decouple reference-response shaping from robust stabilization, thereby providing a standardized actuator interface for reinforcement learning policies. As a result, policies trained only with the prescribed reference model can be deployed zero-shot on real hardware without task-level fine-tuning or learned actuator models. We validate the approach on a single-joint high-gear-ratio servo under external loads and a 7-DOF robotic arm reaching task, where actuator reality shaping substantially reduces sim-to-real tracking error and improves zero-shot task performance compared with standard servo-control and representative real-to-sim-to-real baselines. We further demonstrate zero-shot transfer on a wheeled-legged robot driving over a slope and a humanoid robot walking, suggesting that actuator reality shaping can serve as a reusable interface for robot learning across diverse hardware platforms. Project page: https://syamamori.github.io/ActuatorRealityShaping.github.io/
papers.full_text: Sim-to-real transfer in robot learning is often limited by discrepancies between the ideal actuator dynamics assumed during policy training and the nonlinear, hardware-dependent behavior of physical motors. While conventional approaches attempt to bridge this gap by increasing simulator fidelity through system identification, domain randomization, or learned actuator models, we introduce an alternative paradigm: actuator reality shaping. Instead of modifying the simulator to match the real world, our method shapes the closed-loop behavior of physical actuators to match the idealized second-order reference dynamics used in simulation. By equipping each joint with a two-degree-of-freedom feedforward–feedback controller, we decouple reference-response shaping from robust stabilization, thereby providing a standardized actuator interface for reinforcement learning policies. As a result, policies trained only with the prescribed reference model can be deployed zero-shot on real hardware without task-level fine-tuning or learned actuator models. We validate the approach on a singlejoint high-gear-ratio servo under external loads and a 7-DOF robotic arm reaching task, where actuator reality shaping substantially reduces sim-to-real tracking error and improves zero-shot task performance compared with standard servocontrol and representative real-to-sim-to-real baselines. We further demonstrate zero-shot transfer on a wheeled-legged robot driving over a slope and a humanoid robot walking, suggesting that actuator reality shaping can serve as a reusable interface for robot learning across diverse hardware platforms. Project page Keywords: Reinforcement learning for physical robot control, Sim-to-real transfer, Actuator Reality Shaping Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled impressive locomotion and manipulation controllers when trained in GPU-accelerated, large-scale physical simulation. However, bridging the sim-to-real gap, the performance degradation that arises when policies trained in simulation are deployed on physical hardware, remains a central challenge in robot learning. A major source of this gap lies at the actuator level. While rigid-body simulators often model joints as ideal torque sources or simplified servo systems, real actuators exhibit friction, stiction, backlash, transmission compliance, inertia mismatch, saturation, and electromechanical delays. These unmodeled effects distort the relationship between commanded and realized joint motion, causing policies optimized in simulation to drive the physical robot along unintended trajectories. The resulting mismatch can degrade task performance, amplify tracking errors, and, in dynamic tasks, destabilize the robot. The dominant strategy for reducing the sim-to-real gap has been to make the simulator more realistic. Domain randomization (DR) trains policies over randomized physical parameters so that the real system is likely to lie within the training distribution. Although effective in many settings, this robustness often comes at the cost of task-specific performance, since policies must succeed ① Training in simulation RL policy Sim model (2nd-order PD dynamics) goal state 2-DoF driver layer — per joint @ 500 Hz 2-DoF controller Actuator command goal transfer reference model ideal / simulated real hardware driver layer RL policy deploy zero-shot shaped response ② Deployment on real hardware Figure 1: Actuator reality shaping. We make the real actuator behave like the simulator’s ideal model, rather than the reverse. (Top) simulation with the ideal second-order reference model; (Bottom) zero-shot hardware deployment, where a per-joint 2-DoF driver shapes the response so that θ ≈ θref. across a broad range of dynamics rather than exploit a precise actuator model. A complementary line of work augments the simulator with physics-based or learned actuator models identified from input–output data, or learns online adaptation modules that infer latent environment or actuator parameters during deployment. Despite their success, these approaches share a common dependency: they adapt the simulation or policy to a particular hardware distribution. As a result, they typically require hardware-specific data collection or identification, which must be repeated when actuators are replaced, degrade over time, or are transferred to a different robot platform. This dependency limits the reusability of policies trained in simulation and motivates an alternative interface that standardizes the actuator behavior seen by the policy, rather than continually adapting the simulator to each hardware instance. We propose an alternative perspective: actuator reality shaping. Instead of modifying the simulator to match each physical actuator, we modify the low-level actuator controller so that the hardware presents to the policy the same reference dynamics used during simulation. As illustrated in Figure 1, an RL policy is trained in simulation against an idealized second-order actuator model, and is then deployed zero-shot on hardware, where a per-joint 2-DoF driver shapes the physical actuator response to match the prescribed reference dynamics. Concretely, we introduce a two-degreeof-freedom (2-DoF) controller at each joint driver. Here, “two-degree-of-freedom” is a controltheoretic term: it denotes a controller with two independent design freedoms, typically realized as a feedforward path and a feedback path. This structure allows the reference-response behavior and robust stabilization against disturbances and modeling errors to be designed separately. The feedforward path specifies the desired closed-loop dynamics seen in simulation, while the feedback path compensates for disturbances and residual actuator-model mismatch. We detail these two paths in Section 4 and Figure 2. The resulting driver layer encourages the real joint to follow the same second-order reference dynamics assumed during policy training, thereby providing a standardized actuator interface between the RL policy and the physical hardware. Consequently, a policy trained against this reference model in simulation can be deployed on the real system without task-level fine-tuning or learned actuator models, as long as the physical actuator can track the prescribed dynamics within its bandwidth and saturation limits. The resulting 2-DoF layer plays a role analogous to a device driver: it hides hardware-specific actuator behavior behind a common interface exposed to the policy. In our case, this interface is dy- namical rather than software-based: the policy interacts with the prescribed second-order reference model used in simulation, while the low-level driver compensates for the physical actuator dynamics. This separation provides three practical advantages. First, it enables policy-level hardware abstraction: the same policy can be reused across compatible actuator platforms by redesigning or retuning only the low-level driver, rather than retraining the policy. Second, it provides a smooth learning interface: because the policy is trained against a consistent, idealized actuator response, policy optimization is less exposed to hardware-specific nonlinearities such as friction, backlash, and delay. Third, it improves modularity: the driver can be designed from a compact actuator description, such as the torque constant, rotor inertia, and bandwidth limits, without requiring task-level real-world rollouts or learned actuator models. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. We introduce the actuator reality shaping paradigm for sim-to-real transfer in robot learning, and derive a 2-DoF control architecture that shapes the closed-loop actuator response to match a prescribed simulator reference model. 2. We validate the proposed architecture through single-joint tracking experiments with controlled disturbance injection, and demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a 7-DOF robotic-arm reaching task. We compare against the factory cascaded servo controller, a tuned PID controller, and a learned Delta Action baseline (ASAP ). 3. We further evaluate the generality of the approach through additional zero-shot transfer demonstrations on a wheeled-legged robot with velocity-controlled wheels and a full humanoid robot performing stable forward walking. Related Work Sim-to-Real Transfer in Robot Learning Existing sim-to-real methods fall into three groups. Domain randomization (DR) trains under randomized parameters so the real system lies within the training distribution, but yields conservative worst-case policies and large simulation budgets; adaptive variants such as update the distribution from real rollouts, Rapid Motor distills an online module that infers environment parameters from proprioceptive history, and learns a Delta Action model from real rollouts to compensate the dynamics mismatch at the policy level. Actuator modeling instead augments the simulator with a model identified from hardware data—a black-box network or a few interpretable parameters (rotor inertia, friction, damping)—and implicitly assumes a small residual gap: most demonstrations use quasi-direct-drive actuators with low gear ratios, whose torque response approximates an ideal current source. High-gear-ratio joints violate this assumption, as reflected friction, stiction, and backlash dominate the joint torque and cannot be captured as a simple parametric perturbation. Data-driven system identification estimates environment parameters online and conditions the controller on them, with roots in classical adaptive control and biped-locomotion work refining a bootstrap controller against a data-driven model, or trains an environment-aware policy with an online-identified latent code. All these share a structural cost: hardware-specific data and/or online identification that must be repeated when the hardware changes. We take the dual perspective—rather than identifying the hardware so the policy adapts to it, we shape the hardware’s closed-loop response at the driver level so the policy perceives a fixed, simulator-defined plant on every platform; even high-gear-ratio joints emulate the ideal reference plant, with residual error absorbed at runtime by the disturbance observer and integral feedback. Two-Degree-of-Freedom and Model Reference Control The 2-DoF control architecture decouples reference tracking from disturbance rejection through independent feedforward and feedback designs, and is commonly combined with a disturbance observer to reject friction and load. However, these approaches operate at the level of individual joint control and are therefore insufficient for generating whole-body motion. As a result, their use as a sim-to-real interface layer has not been sufficiently explored. Our design shares the reference-model layer idea with a fixed-gain 2-DoF controller derived from a minimal actuator model, avoiding convergence monitoring, gain scheduling, and adaptation–saturation stability issues, and requiring no hardware adaptation data. Problem Formulation Markov Decision Process in Actuator We consider a Multi-DoF robot with n revolute joints actuated by DC motors. An RL policy π: O → A maps an observation ot ∈ O to a goal joint angle ¯θt ∈ A. In simulation, joint j is governed by a PD controller acting on the goal joint angle: Isim¨θj = Kp(¯θj − θj) − D ˙θj + fj, (1) where Isim, Kp, D are the simulated inertia, proportional gain, and damping coefficient, and fj is the net external joint torque. The transition operator of the MDP is defined by the dynamics (1), and the policy π is optimized against this operator using RL algorithm, e.g. PPO. Actuator Gap In simulation, (1) implicitly assumes that the commanded torque τcmd = Kp(¯θj − θj) − D ˙θj is produced instantaneously at the joint. On real hardware, joint j is driven by a motor with dynamics: Jreal¨θj = Kτi(ij − id,j) − dreal ˙θj − τf,j( ˙θj) − τext,j, (2) where Jreal is the actual rotor inertia (including gear reflection), Kτi the torque constant, ij the current command, id,j a disturbance current (e.g., cogging), dreal the viscous damping, τf,j( ˙θ) a velocity-dependent friction term (Coulomb friction and stiction), and τext,j an external load torque. Linearizing the mechanical dynamics around the operating point and taking the torque-to-angle relation, we describe each joint by a plant transfer function P(s) = θj(s)/τj(s). From the inertia and damping terms of (1) and (2) we obtain Psim(s) = Isims2+Ds, Preal(s) = Jreals2+dreals, where the nonlinear and exogenous terms of (2)—the velocity-dependent friction τf,j( ˙θj), the disturbance current Kτiid,j, and the external load τext,j—enter Preal additively as a lumped disturbance torque. The actuator gap is the multiplicative uncertainty of the real plant relative to the simulated one, ∆Pj(s) = Preal(s) Psim(s) − 1 = Isims + D Jreals + dreal − 1, (3) so that Preal(s) = � 1 + ∆Pj(s) � Psim(s). This dimensionless gap captures the inertia mismatch Jreal − Isim and the damping mismatch dreal − D, while the friction, cogging, and external load act as additive disturbances on top of ∆Pj(s). It is the same model error ∆P that the controller in Sec. 4 attenuates. Our objective is to design a controller that suppresses the effect of the actuator gap, ∆Pj → 0 and the disturbance influence, so that the closed loop reduces to the simulated reference dynamics; consequently ∥θj(t) − θref,j(t)∥ → 0 for all bounded disturbances τext,j, where θref,j is the output of the simulator reference model (1) driven by the same policy goal joint angles ¯θj. If this objective is achieved, the policy π perceives identical dynamics in simulation and on the real hardware, enabling zero-shot transfer. Method Figure 2 shows the proposed per-joint actuator reality shaping architecture: a cascaded two-degreeof-freedom (2-DoF) controller—a position outer loop wrapped around a velocity inner loop and augmented with a disturbance observer (DOB)—that drives the real motor to reproduce the simulator’s reference dynamics. We detail each component in the following subsections. Two-Degree-of-Freedom Controller We adopt the standard 2-DoF control structure to independently specify the reference tracking and disturbance rejection characteristics. Let P(s) denote the plant block. The control input is: u = F(s) ˆP(s) r + K(s)e, e = F(s)r − y, (4) Goal + Feedback Feedforward PID feedback + + + external load torque Actuator Model DOB − 2-DOF controller (pos.) disturbance observer real actuator 2-DoF Controller Velocity 2-DoF Controller (vel.) The closed-loop transfer function from reference to output and from disturbance to output is: y = � 1 + ∆P 1 + PK � � �� � ≈1 Fr + P 1 + PK � �� � sensitivity d, (5) where d is the input disturbance torque; the step-by-step derivation is given in Appendix B. When the feedback gain K is sufficiently large to compensate for the model error (∆P), the output tracks y ∼ F r regardless of the disturbance rejection loop, so F can be designed independently to match the simulator’s reference dynamics. We choose: F1(s) = Kp Isims2 + Ds + Kp, F2(s) = α s + α, (6) so that the outer-loop plant P1 ≈ F2/s, since the inner velocity loop’s closed-loop response closely follows the reference model F2 under the inner-loop 2-DoF velocity control. The feedback block K(s) must include an integrator to guarantee zero steady-state tracking error in the presence of constant disturbances, by the internal model principle. We use: K(s) = kp + ki s + kds, (7) a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller. Disturbance Observer The 2-DoF controller is augmented with a disturbance observer (DOB) that estimates the disturbance torque ˆτd from the commanded torque and the measured velocity through a low-pass filter with cutoff frequency αdob, and cancels it by subtracting a compensation torque ˆτd from the commanded current before it is sent to the driver, attenuating the residual model error ∆P below αdob. The detailed derivation, including the filtered disturbance estimate and the resulting effective plant, is provided in Appendix C, and the reconstruction accuracy of the estimated disturbance is reported in Appendix D. Cascaded Position-Velocity Control For position-controlled revolute joints (e.g., arm joints), we cascade two 2-DoF loops. The inner loop is a velocity control loop with plant ˆP2 = 1/(Js + d) and reference model matched to the velocity response F2, where J is the nominal inertia and d is the nominal viscous damping. The outer loop is a position control loop whose reference model F1 is the full second-order response (1) and plant P1 ∼ ˆP1 = F2/s. The outer loop outputs a goal joint velocity ¯˙θ that serves as the reference for the inner loop. Implementation details (per-step procedure and DOB low-pass filter) and the controller parameters used in all experiments are provided in Appendix E (Table 2). Experimental Setup We evaluate actuator reality shaping on platforms of increasing task complexity: a single-joint testbench (reference-model tracking under static and dynamic disturbances), a 7-DOF arm (endeffector reaching under inter-joint coupling), and a wheeled-legged robot and humanoid robot (zeroshot driving and bipedal walking across embodiments). Hardware Platform. We evaluate on three custom-built, in-house platforms: a 7-DOF robotic arm; a wheeled-legged robot (31 DOF), a tripod of four 7-DOF arms rigidly coupled at a central body, three terminating in wheel actuators for combined manipulation and locomotion; and a humanoid robot (22 DOF) with two 6-DOF legs, a 2-DOF waist, and two 4-DOF arms. Their IsaacSim models are built from URDF files whose kinematic trees come directly from the original CAD data. Because these models lack the implicit parameter tuning of commercial robots and vendor-supplied simulation assets, the sim-to-real gap on our platforms is considerably more severe than on off-the-shelf hardware, making them a stringent testbed for zero-shot transfer. All single-joint experiments are conducted on a testbench using the same joint actuator unit deployed on the robots: a high-gear-ratio servo with a cycloidal gear reducer (Dynamixel YM070, 99:1, ROBOTIS), so that the identified motor parameters and controller gains transfer directly to the multi-joint experiments without re-tuning. The YM070 is used for the single-joint tracking experiments, the robotic arm reaching task, and the wheeled-legged robot experiments, whereas the Dynamixel PH54 (501.9:1, ROBOTIS) is used for the humanoid walking experiment. The high gear ratio reflects link-side inertia back through N 2 (N=99 for the YM070, N=501.9 for the PH54), so motor-side inertia dominates the joint-level dynamics by orders of magnitude. Inter-joint inertial coupling is therefore small relative to the motor-side inertia and appears at the DOB as a low-frequency bounded perturbation within the rejection bandwidth, validating the per-joint decentralized DOB assumption. Simulator and Policy Training. The simulator is Isaac with joint dynamics implemented as (1), and policies are trained within the IsaacLab learning framework. RL policies are trained using; the actor-critic architecture and per-task training settings are summarized in Appendix F (Table 3). For the humanoid walking task, we build on the public implementation of, replacing only the actuator model and low-level controller with our 2-DoF+DOB design while keeping the policy architecture, reward terms, and training pipeline unchanged. The physical-parameter randomization ranges used for the humanoid walking and wheeled-robot reaching tasks are listed in Appendix G. Comparison Methods. We compare against the following baselines, all running at the same 500 Hz driver-level control frequency. To isolate the DOB’s contribution, we report two configurations of our method: 2-DoF, the feedforward–feedback controller (4) alone, and 2-DoF+DOB, the same controller augmented with the disturbance observer (see Appendix C); elsewhere we refer to the method simply as 2-DoF, as the DOB is an optional enhancement rather than a separate architecture. PID Cascade: the servo’s factory default controller—a multi-stage (cascaded) position–velocity– current PID loop running on the drive firmware. It is a feedback-only, 1-DoF controller with no feedforward path. This represents the standard servo-controller baseline a practitioner obtains out of the box without any actuator-aware redesign. Simple PD: a single-loop PD controller (no feedforward, no DOB, no cascade) that outputs the motor current command directly from the joint state,i = kp(θref − θ) − kd ˙θ, with gains kp, kd manually tuned for stable tracking on the real hardware. Concretely, a Delta Action policy π∆ is learned so that the deployed action augments the base policy output, a = π(s) + π∆(s), (8) where π∆ is fitted to minimize the mismatch between the simulated transition under a and the observed real-world transition, i.e. minπ∆ E � ∥fsim(s, a) − s′ real∥2�. Unlike our method, ASAP requires hardware-specific data collection to fit the Delta Action model. Results Single-Axis Tracking. We compare the baselines (PID cascade, Simple PD, 2-DoF) with our 2- DoF+DOB on a YM070 servo, taking the simulator reference dynamics (1) as the target. The phase portraits of the position error ∆θ = θ − θref and velocity error ∆ ˙θ = ˙θ − ˙θref (Appendix A, Fig. 5a) show that the PID Cascade and Simple PD controllers leave a large sim-to-real gap—their position loops track the commanded goal angle rather than the reference dynamics, producing a systematic bias along ∆ ˙θ—whereas the 2-DoF and 2-DoF+DOB clouds stay near the origin owing to the feedforward filter F, which reduces phase lag without overshoot. 2-DoF alone leaves a slight position offset, indicating the DOB further suppresses disturbance torques such as friction. Over a 20 s sinusoidal reference (20◦ amplitude, 2.5 s period; 5 runs), the 2-DoF+DOB controller reduces the mean position deviation by 96.3% and 94.5% relative to the PID Cascade and Simple PD baselines, and the mean velocity deviation—the cascade’s dominant error mode—by 99.1% relative to the cascade (Table 1). The 2-DoF and 2-DoF+DOB results are similar in single-axis tracking; the DOB’s advantage instead becomes pronounced in the reaching task. Reaching Task. The end-effector error on the reaching task, where the 7-DOF arm tracks a lemniscate (figure-eight) trajectory, is reported in the phase portrait of Appendix A (Fig. 5b); the policy trained against the ideal reference model (1) in IsaacSim transfers zero-shot to real hardware via 2-DoF+DOB, and we compare the deployed real-robot trajectory against the simulated one. Controllers other than 2-DoF track the target poorly, and as before the DOB further improves tracking. Figure 3 compares our method against, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that corrects the simulator from real-world data and retrains the policy. The ASAP residual (8) reduced the simto-real gap, but to do so it output larger actions than the base policy π, destabilizing training in simulation (loss curves in Appendix H); its real-robot performance was thus not substantially better than the untuned factory Default. Our method instead attains good zero-shot performance without any fine-tuning. Over the steady-state window of the lemniscate (5 runs, Table 1), the 2-DoF+DOB controller attains the lowest end-effector deviation—a 96.5% reduction relative to the factory PID cascade; the DOB accounts for a further 50% over 2-DoF alone, and 2-DoF+DOB reduces the error by 72% over the tuned Simple PD baseline, since uncompensated friction in the PD and cascaded controllers introduces a systematic offset the policy cannot anticipate. (a) End-effector position error (b) End-effector orientation error Figure 3: Comparison with on the reaching task Figure 4: Zero-shot demonstrations on other embodiments. The per-joint 2-DoF driver layer applied to (a) a wheeled legged robot climbing a slope and (b) a humanoid robot’s zero-shot walk. Zero-Shot Demonstrations on Other Embodiments. We further deploy the 2-DoF driver layer on two other platforms; time-lapse sequences are shown in Fig. 4. Wheeled legged robot. Applied to the velocity-controlled wheel actuators, a policy trained against the reference model transfers zero-shot, climbing a slope (Fig. 4a) whose height must be inferred from per-joint states and IMU posture alone, difficult for poorly backdrivable high-gear-ratio servos, yet the 2-DoF controller succeeds by reproducing the simulator’s compliant spring-damper behavior. Humanoid robot. Using a different servo (PH54), we train a walking policy with the off-the-shelf framework, swapping only the actuator model for the ideal reference model. The policy transfers without hardware-specific tuning and the robot takes stable forward steps (Fig. 4b), showing the approach carries over to a high-DOF, dynamically balancing whole-body platform. Limitations The method treats the joint-axis inertia as a constant Isim, whereas it depends on the whole-body configuration Isim(q); this is negligible at high gear ratios but not for quasi-direct-drive actuators, where accounting for it (e.g., via Model Reference Adaptive Control) is a promising direction. The nominal J and Kτi still require a coarse estimate, and whether the approach extends to strongly nonlinear hardware remains open. Conclusion We have presented actuator reality shaping: a per-joint two-degree-of-freedom controller that, using only a minimal motor model, drives real actuators to replicate the simulator’s second-order reference dynamics. By relocating the sim-to-real adaptation burden to a transparent, hardware-agnostic driver layer, it enables zero-shot transfer without hardware-specific data.

papers.title: Learning End-to-End Control for Omnidirectional Aerial Motion on Overactuated Tilt-rotor Quadrotors
papers.abstract: While reinforcement learning (RL) has been successfully applied to conventional quadrotors for agile and robust flight, whether actuator-level RL can be reliably deployed on tilt-rotor aerial robots remains an open question, as the hybrid actuation coupling brushless rotors with rotational joints introduces a substantially harder sim-to-real gap. In this work, we propose an end-to-end RL framework for omnidirectional motion control on overactuated tilt-rotor quadrotors, directly mapping target poses to joint and rotor commands. The learning framework combines actuator-level simulation with an asymmetric actor-critic architecture for 6D pose-reaching. For reliable sim-to-real transfer on the hybrid actuation, we integrate system identification with minimal yet physically grounded domain randomization. The trained policy is deployed zero-shot on real hardware and evaluated across waypoint hovering, external disturbances, payload variation and trajectory tracking, together with simulated traversal of allocation-singular configurations. The policy is compared with a state-of-the-art NMPC baseline: NMPC attains lower steady-state position error, whereas the RL policy offers a more uniform orientation error across evaluations, transitions between poses faster, and requires less onboard computation.

Index Terms—Reinforcement Learning, Aerial Systems: Mechanics and Control, Motion Control I. INTRODUCTION Aerial robots have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a wide range of applications. In particular, quadrotors have been extensively deployed in diverse real-world missions, including inspection, delivery, and search and rescue. Despite their success, conventional quadrotors are inherently underactuated and cannot independently regulate position and orientation, which limits their applicability to advanced aerial interaction. To address this limitation, omnidirectional aerial robots have recently attracted growing attention for their ability to perform full six-degree-of-freedom (6D) motion,,. Among the various designs, tilt-rotor platforms stand out by actively reorienting individual thrust vectors, attaining high actuation efficiency without internal force cancellation,,. However, this expanded capability comes at the cost of substantially increased system complexity. The strong coupling between joint and rotor dynamics, combined with the highly flexible omnidirectional motion capability (Fig. 1), poses fundamental challenges for motion control. Model-based control has long been the mainstream approach for tilt-rotor aerial robots, with geometric control,, and Model Predictive Control (MPC), as the most representative formulations. These methods typically adopt a sequential structure, as illustrated in Fig. 2. For an aerial robot expressed in the body frame with mass m, inertia Jb, linear velocity vb, and angular velocity ωb, the rigid-body dynamics are written as: � Fb τb � + � Fd τd � = � mI3 0 Jb �� ˙vb ˙ωb � + � ωb × mvb ωb × Jbωb � (1) where [Fb τb]⊤ denotes the body wrench produced by the actuators and [Fd τd]⊤ represents the external disturbance wrench. For tilt-rotor platforms, the body wrench is jointly produced by joint positions qj and rotor thrusts fr, coupled through the allocation matrix Aα: �Fb τb �⊤ = Aα (qj) �fr,1 fr,2 · · ·�⊤ (2) Actuator commands are then recovered by inverting this allocation mapping. Under nominal conditions, the hierarchical framework achieves accurate pose regulation and offers strong layer-wise interpretability. Fig. 2: Model-based control framework for tiltable aerial robots. Beyond accuracy and interpretability, this decomposition keeps each subproblem solvable at the control rate, enabling onboard deployment. However, several characteristics of model-based methods motivate complementary research directions: (i) the model must stay tractable within the online control period, so it is often reduced under simplifying assumptions; unmodeled dynamics and external disturbances [Fd τd] are then handled by dedicated observers and compensated through the allocator, whereas learning-based formulations can propagate the dynamic model offline, through large-scale training-time exposure; (ii) the allocation matrix Aα becomes ill-conditioned at certain joint configurations, which prior work has addressed through explicit regularization or actuator-dynamics integration,. These observations motivate us to investigate whether a policy trained offline can directly operate actuators while subsuming planning, control, and allocation within a single policy. Learning-based approaches have emerged as a promising alternative to model-based control and have showcased impressive performance across various aerial robotics tasks. pioneered actuator-level reinforcement learning (RL) for quadrotor waypoint tracking. demonstrated robust disturbance rejection under strong winds via deep learning combined with meta-learning. and achieved aggressive quadrotor flight comparable to human champions in drone racing. trained a single policy that generalizes across quadrotor platforms with diverse physical parameters and rotor configurations. While these studies highlight the potential of learningbased control, they are largely confined to fixed-rotor platforms. To the best of our knowledge, data-driven control for tilt-rotor robots remains significantly underexplored, with only a few works integrating learned components into, guiding policy training with a model-based action prior, or fine-tuning actuator-level policies with real-world data for sim-to-real transfer. These preliminary efforts suggest that learning-based control is promising for tilt-rotor platforms, but also expose the substantial challenges in learning formulation and sim-to-real transfer on such complex systems. Adopting RL on a new robotic platform fundamentally requires answering two questions: (1) what learning formulation fits the platform, and (2) how can the trained policy be reliably transferred from simulation to the real system? Prior work on fixed-rotor quadrotors has explored three action-space abstractions that occupy distinct points along the trade-off between sim-to-real transferability and the breadth of system dynamics they can exploit, as illustrated in Fig. 3. The Linear Velocity (LV) abstraction is the most high-level: it transfers easily with velocity controller but underexploits the platform’s full dynamic capabilities. The Collective Thrust and Bodyrates (CTBR) abstraction strikes a balance between transferability and dynamic expressiveness, and is widely adopted on fixedrotor systems,; however, applying CTBR to tilt-rotor platforms still requires a low-level allocator beneath the policy, leaving the singularity-prone allocation problem unresolved. The Single-Rotor Thrusts (SRT) abstraction operates directly at the actuator level and can holistically capture the platform’s dynamics, but is less commonly used because of the stronger sim-to-real demands it imposes. Fig. 3: Data-driven control frameworks for quadrotors. LV: rely on a control stack to process velocity commands. CTBR: require a feedback regulator to process rotor thrusts. SRT: directly command rotor thrusts. Given the highly flexible motion capability and strong jointrotor coupling of tilt-rotor platforms, we adopt an actuatorlevel abstraction analogous to SRT and propose an end-to-end RL framework for 6D pose-reaching control on overactuated tilt-rotor quadrotors. The policy directly maps the target pose and current state to joint position and rotor thrust commands with a single policy. However, this approach introduces a more severe sim-to-real gap, further exacerbated by the hybrid actuation system that couples brushless rotors with servodriven joints. To bridge this gap, we integrate actuator system identification with minimal yet physically grounded domain randomization into a sim-to-real pipeline, validated through extensive real-world experiments. The main contributions are summarized as follows: • An end-to-end reinforcement learning framework is proposed, which produces joint and rotor commands from a single policy on overactuated tilt-rotor quadrotors, enabling actuator-level 6D pose-reaching control. • A sim-to-real pipeline tailored to the hybrid actuation is introduced, integrating actuator system identification, control-architecture latency alignment, and minimal yet physically grounded domain randomization. • Zero-shot deployment across five real-world flight scenarios and a simulated traversal of allocation-singular configurations, together with a matched comparison against a servo-integrated NMPC baseline on the same platform and software stack, in which the policy holds a more uniform orientation error at lower online computation. Fig. 4: Overall framework for simulation, RL training, and deployment. Robot: Rotor modules (blue, target thrust f ∗ r → real thrust fr and torque τr), joint modules (red, joint position commands q∗ j → position feedback qj), and system latency (green arrows) are modeled to construct physically consistent simulation environments. Training: The policy is trained under an asymmetric actor-critic framework and dynamics randomization (green) is integrated according to models and deployment scheme. Deployment: Trained policy is deployed on real robot platform with a consistent system architecture. The robot’s state is estimated by fusing data from a motion capture system (MoCap) and an onboard IMU using an Extended Kalman filter (EKF). II. METHOD The proposed RL framework for pose-reaching control is designed in accordance with the real robot platform and deployment scheme, as shown in Fig. 4. A. Preliminaries 1) Platform Introduction: The tilt-rotor quadrotor platform consists of four rotor modules, each mounted at the tip of one arm. Each module uses a three-bladed 9 in propeller driven by a T-Motor AT2814 KV900 brushless DC motor and is connected to the arm through a single-degree-offreedom rotational joint actuated by a DYNAMIXEL XC330 T181-T servomotor. This design enables full 6-DOF wrench generation; the detailed physical parameters are listed in Appendix IV-A. 2) Task Definition: The control task is defined as reaching a target pose [p∗ w, θ∗ b] in SE(3) and maintaining stability thereafter, by directly commanding the joint positions qj and rotor thrusts fr. In contrast to velocity-tracking or body-wrench regulation, this pose-level formulation grants the policy full authority over the transition trajectory, prompting it to discover efficient motion strategies through trial-and-error interactions. 3) Problem Formulation: The proposed RL control problem is formulated as an infinite-horizon Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), defined by the tuple (S, O, A, T, d0, r, γ). Here, s ∈ S denotes the full system state, o ∈ O represents the partial observation, and a ∈ A is action. The initial state distribution is given by d0, and the state transition dynamics are described by T (st+1|st, at). The reward function is denoted by r(st, at) with discount factor γ ∈ [0, 1). The objective is to learn a policy πΘ(a|o), parameterized by Θ, that maximizes the expected cumulative discounted reward E [�∞ t=0 γtr(st, at)]. B. Training Scheme 1) Observation and Action Space: The policy action at time-step t is defined as at = � aj,t, ar,t � ∈ R8, (3) where aj,t ∈ R4 and ar,t ∈ R4 are the joint and rotor-thrust components, respectively. They are mapped to the target joint positions q∗ j,t and rotor thrusts f ∗ r,t as q∗ j,t = cjaj,t, f ∗ r,t = crar,t + Cf, (4) where cj and cr are scale coefficients and Cf is the nominal hovering thrust that approximately balances gravity. Centering the action around Cf lets the policy issue both positive and negative thrust adjustments about hover, facilitating early-stage exploration and yielding smoother commands. The joint and rotor models are obtained through system identification, as detailed in Sec. II-C2 and Sec. II-C3. The policy observation ot ∈ R33 at time-step t is ot = � vb,t, ωb,t, p∗ b,t, Rb,t, R∗ b,t, qj,t, at−1 �, (5) where the subscript b denotes quantities in the robot base frame. vb,t, ωb,t ∈ R3 are the base linear and angular velocities. p∗ b,t ∈ R3 is the world-frame target p∗ w transformed into the current body frame. The current and target orientations Rb,t, R∗ b,t ∈ R6 are encoded by the first two columns of their rotation matrices, a continuous representation that improves learning stability over quaternion or Euler-angle parameterizations. qj,t ∈ R4 contains the feedback joint positions, and at−1 is the previous action. Since the deployed policy has access only to partial observations, we adopt an asymmetric actor-critic framework: the actor is conditioned on ot, while the critic is fed with a richer state st ∈ R41 for better value estimation, st = � vb,t, ωb,t, p∗ b,t, Rb,t, R∗ b,t, qj,t, fr,t, τr,t, at−1 �, (6) where the privileged variables are the rotor thrusts fr,t and the corresponding reaction torques τr,t ∈ R4. 2) Reward Function: The control objective is to drive the system toward a desired pose while maintaining smooth and stable motion. We characterize desirable performance as fast convergence to the target pose with reduced oscillations and moderate control effort, in line with criteria commonly adopted in model-based control. Accordingly, the reward function consists of: (1) pose-reaching terms that encourage rapid convergence toward the desired pose, and (2) regularization terms that promote smooth and stable motion. Towards Position encourages the robot to move toward the target position, while Towards Pose promotes orientation alignment as the position error decreases. Reach Position and Reach Pose provide sparse bonuses once the robot enters the specified thresholds and remains stable. Linear Velocity and Angular Velocity penalties discourage aggressive motion and promote stable flight. Unlike the pose-reaching formulations commonly adopted in legged robot learning, we avoid explicit time- or reference-velocity-based terms that enforce convergence within a prescribed duration; instead, the reward design balances task completion, energy efficiency, and motion smoothness, allowing the policy to autonomously discover control strategies that achieve agile yet stable pose conver- gence. Additional regularization terms penalize actuator-limit violations, abrupt action changes, excessive thrust power, and large joint accelerations. The z-Axis Align auxiliary reward promotes reaching the desired tilt angle. Thrust Allocation encourages an even distribution of rotor thrusts across varying base orientations, thereby balancing actuator workloads. Early Termination suppresses inefficient exploration of failure episodes by aborting upon ground collision or exceeding the altitude bound. 3) Initial State Distribution: The desired position p∗ w ∈ R3 is drawn uniformly within a 4 m × 4 m × 3 m region and transformed into the body frame as p∗ b. The desired orientation θ∗ b is sampled to broadly cover SO(3) by first drawing the target body +z-axis on the unit sphere and then applying a yaw rotation uniformly in [−π, π] about it. The robot is initialized at the world origin with zero linear and angular velocities, default hovering thrust Cf, and orientation sampled in the same manner of θ∗ b. The initial joint position qj,0 requires particular care, since static hovering is feasible only at specific joint–thrust configurations. Initializing with default (fixed) joint configurations tends to converge to local optima, while uniform random sampling can lead to inefficient convergence. To encourage exploration while maintaining convergence efficiency, qj,0 is stratified across parallel environments into four equally weighted groups: (i) all joints at −π, (ii) all at 0, (iii) all at π, and (iv) each joint independently sampled from {−π, 0, π}. C. Sim-to-Real Transfer 1) System Latency: System latency is unavoidable on realworld platforms and can degrade control performance or even induce divergent oscillations. To bridge this gap, we explicitly model the dominant delays during training: the commanded q∗ j,t and f ∗ r,t are applied to the simulated actuators with an actuation delay, and the corresponding joint feedback qj,t is returned with a sensing delay. The base velocities vb,t and ωb,t further carry an algorithmic delay from the EKF state estimator, which fuses motion-capture and IMU measurements. These delays are estimated by collecting real platform data. 2) Rotor Model: The rotor module serves as the primary actuator of the aerial robot. Since rotor thrust dynamics are highly nonlinear and depend on the coupled effects of motor characteristics, propeller aerodynamics, and supply voltage, accurate first-principles modeling is impractical. We instead identify the rotor thrust and reaction torque empirically by sweeping PWM commands and supply voltages on a 6-axis force-torque sensor, and fit polynomial functions to map the PWM command cmdr and voltage Vr to the generated thrust and torque: fr = fr(cmdr, Vr), τr = CΩfr, (7) where CΩ denotes the torque-to-thrust ratio. During training, the commanded thrust is realized as fr,t = f ∗ r,t and applied as external force and reaction torque on each rotor link. During deployment, the PWM command is recovered through the inverse mapping cmdr,t = f−1 r (f ∗ r,t, Vr). 3) Joint Model: Joint modeling is critical for tilt-rotor quadrotors, since the rotor-generated wrench is steered by the joint positions, distinguishing them from fixed-rotor platforms. Rotational joints in common rigid-body simulators are modeled as DC motors with proportional-derivative (PD) position control: J ¨qj = Kp(q∗ j − qj) − Kd ˙qj, (8) where J is the effective rotational inertia, and Kp, Kd are the stiffness and damping coefficients, respectively. The resulting closed-loop joint dynamics are well-approximated by a second-order transfer function qj(s) q∗ j (s) = Kp Js2 + Kds + Kp, (9) with natural frequency ωn and damping ratio ζ satisfying ω2 n = Kp/J, 2ζωn = Kd/J. (10) We identify ωn and ζ from the measured joint response, then back-compute Kp and Kd for the simulated joints via the relations above. The joint torque and velocity limits are similarly determined experimentally. During deployment, the joint position commands are directly issued as cmdq,t = q∗ j,t. Experimental Setup The training environment is built on Isaac and Isaac, and the policy is optimized with proximal policy optimization (PPO) using the RSL-RL implementation. [deg] Fig. 11: State evolution under continuous rotation through Aα singularities. IV. CONCLUSION This paper presented a sim-to-real reinforcement learning pipeline for SE(3) pose-reaching on overactuated tilt-rotor quadrotors. A single policy directly produces joint and rotor commands for zero-shot real-world deployment with actuatorlevel system identification, latency alignment, and physically grounded domain randomization to bridge the gap induced by the hybrid joint-rotor actuation. Experiments demonstrate consistent performance across waypoint hovering, external disturbances, payload variation, trajectory tracking, and continuous rotation through allocation-singular configurations, the last typically requiring explicit regularization in allocation-based controllers. As the dynamics calculation is performed during training, the policy keeps its online computation minimal, which suits platforms with limited onboard resources and tasks that demand consistent behavior across conditions rather than absolute accuracy. Two limitations remain: the platform model omits aerodynamic effects such as wind drag and inter-rotor downwash, calling for richer real-to-sim modeling; and the reward relies on manually shaped terms to coordinate the joint-rotor dynamics, motivating more principled formulations. Further hardware optimization and control problem formulation are needed to fully unlock the potential of actuator-level policies on tilt-rotor platforms. APPENDIX A. papers.title: Shooting for Contact: Contact-Implicit Multiple Shooting for Dynamic Motion Retargeting
papers.abstract: Motion retargeting approaches often prioritize kinematic similarity over whole-body dynamics, contact consistency, and actuation limits, yielding references that are difficult for reinforcement learning (RL) policies to reproduce, particularly for contact-rich behaviors. We present a contact-implicit, direct simulation-based multiple shooting (DSMS) framework that transforms kinematically feasible references into dynamically feasible whole-body trajectories. By embedding a differentiable simulator within a nonlinear program, DSMS resolves contact, friction, impacts, self-collision, and joint limits internally while enforcing tracking, actuation, and task constraints without prescribing a contact schedule or introducing explicit contact constraints. Compared with existing retargeting methods, DSMS accelerates motion-imitation RL training and yields policies with high success rates and low tracking error. We further demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on the Unitree G1 through command-conditioned walking, jogging, and contact-rich crawling, and a highly dynamic 180-degree jump-turn.
papers.full_text: Motion retargeting approaches often prioritize kinematic similarity over whole-body dynamics, contact consistency, and actuation limits, yielding references that are difficult for reinforcement learning (RL) policies to reproduce, particularly for contact-rich behaviors. We present a contactimplicit, direct simulation-based multiple shooting (DSMS) framework that transforms kinematically feasible references into dynamically feasible whole-body trajectories. By embedding a differentiable simulator within a nonlinear program, DSMS resolves contact, friction, impacts, self-collision, and joint limits internally while enforcing tracking, actuation, and task constraints without prescribing a contact schedule or introducing explicit contact constraints. Compared with existing retargeting methods, DSMS accelerates motionimitation RL training and yields policies with high success rates and low tracking error. We further demonstrate zeroshot sim-to-real transfer on the Unitree G1 through commandconditioned walking, jogging, and contact-rich crawling, and a highly dynamic 180-degree jump-turn. Additional Material: shooting-for-contact.github.io. I. INTRODUCTION Reference motions derived from human demonstrations, reduced-order models, and animation provide powerful priors for learning and control. Recent reference-tracking reinforcement learning (RL) and imitation learning (IL) have demonstrated complex locomotion and whole-body behaviors from motion-capture, animation, and video-generated trajectories –. However, the quality of the learned controller depends strongly on the reference motion,. Most retargeting pipelines prioritize kinematic correspondence, mapping human pose or key-body poses onto the robot while accounting for differences in morphology,. Although this approach can produce visually plausible motions, the resulting trajectories are often not dynamically consistent with robot physics, contacts, or actuation limits. This dynamics mismatch is particularly problematic for contact-rich behaviors, such as crawling, parkour jumping, and rolling, during which the robot may use different body parts for support and balance. A kinematically retargeted motion may contain foot sliding, unrealistic ground penetrations, self-collisions, or actions that require infeasible torques and impulses. RL can sometimes compensate for and robustify these defects, but it must then simultaneously 1The authors are with the Department of Mechanical and Civil Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA, USA. {sesteban,jasonsiu,dmach,junhengl, ames}@caltech.edu and jwb@robotics.caltech.edu. 2The author is with the School of Computing, DePaul University, Chicago, IL, USA. vkurtz1@depaul.edu. *This work was supported by Technology Innovation Institute (TII). Fig. 1: DSMS trajectory optimization solutions in simulation (left) and their corresponding zero-shot hardware realizations on the Unitree G1 (right), shown for velocity-conditioned contact-rich crawling (top) and a 180◦ jump-turn (bottom). discover a feasible realization of the motion and learn to stabilize it. These characteristics make reward tuning difficult: strong tracking rewards pull the policy toward an infeasible reference, while weaker rewards allow the learned behavior to deviate from the intended motion. We propose a method for generating dynamically feasible references for RL. Before policy training, trajectory optimization transforms the original motion into a dynamically consistent reference for the target robot, reasoning over contacts not known a priori and accommodating arbitrary task constraints. The policy then only needs to stabilize a physically meaningful nominal trajectory rather than discover one from a dynamically inconsistent reference. A. Related Works Generating meaningful robot references is challenging because contact-rich humanoid motion is high-dimensional and hybrid. Recent reference-based RL has enabled humanoid robots to reproduce diverse locomotion and whole-body behaviors from human motion data,,. However, such motions are largely generated through kinematic retargeting and geometric correspondence. Other methods improve this stage by allowing interaction-preserving constraints or learned motion refinement,,. Because these pipelines remain largely kinematic, the resulting references can violate the robot’s dynamics, degrading the robustness and convergence of downstream tracking policies,. Several works explicitly improve the physical feasibility of reference motions: bi-level motion imitation alternates between adapting the reference and the tracking policy, OmniTrack uses privileged policy rollouts, and DynaRetarget and employ shooting-based trajectory optimization or sampling-based model-predictive control (MPC) in simulation. However, these approaches either couple reference refinement to policy training or rely on sampling, which complicates enforcing hard task constraints. Kinodynamic retargeting avoids both but requires a prescribed contact sequence. Nonlinear programs based on direct collocation and multiple shooting have shown promise for stabilizing highly dynamic and underactuated systems. However, in their standard forms, these transcriptions do not resolve contact implicitly and instead require prescribed contact modes or explicit contact constraints. Contact-implicit trajectory optimization (CITO) provides an appealing basis for ensuring dynamic feasibility,, since the optimizer is free to make or break contacts as needed while staying close to a reference motion. However, many CITO methods require explicit contact pairs, complementarity constraints or relaxations, smooth contact models, or contact-force variables, –. Additionally, many aim primarily at MPC, where full convergence and tight constraints are compromised for speed,. Related shooting-based methods require differentiable simulations for whole-body MPC, while derivative-free methods such as predictive sampling provide a simple alternative for contact-rich behavior synthesis,. More broadly, differentiable simulators obtain useful sensitivities through regularized contact, implicit differentiation of hard-contact solves, or analytical differentiation of collision and friction –. B. Contributions This work introduces direct simulation-based multishooting (DSMS), a nonlinear program transcription for dynamics-aware retargeting of contact-rich humanoid motions in which the discrete transition map of a differentiable simulator defines the whole-body dynamics between shooting nodes. Contact, friction, self-collision, and actuation limits are thus handled internally by the simulator rather than through a traditional contact-implicit formulation. Our main contributions are: • A general direct simulation-based multi-shooting framework for whole-body dynamics and contact-implicit motion retargeting. • A unified pipeline that transforms kinematically feasible trajectories into whole-body dynamically feasible references and that synthesizes command-conditioned periodic gait libraries from a few short motion clips. • For motion-imitation RL, a numerical study of how references generated with reduced-order, kinodynamic, and our full-order optimization affect downstream policy training and tracking performance. • Hardware demonstrations of (i) twist commandconditioned humanoid walking, jogging, and contactrich crawling, and (ii) a highly dynamic 180◦ jump-turn motion. II. PRELIMINARIES A. Whole-Body Dynamics We consider legged robots that achieve locomotion by intermittently making and breaking contact with their environment. In particular, we are interested in contact-rich behaviors in which the robot may use any part of its body to generate motion. We define the state as x:= (q, v) ∈ TQ, where q ∈ Q ⊆ Rnq denotes the generalized configuration and v ∈ TqQ ⊆ Rnv the generalized velocity. The whole-body (WB) continuous-time dynamics can be written as M(q) ˙v + H(q, v) = Bτ + J⊤ c (q)λ, (1) where M: Q → Rnv×nv is the mass–inertia matrix, H: TQ → Rnv collects Coriolis, centrifugal, and gravitational terms, B ∈ Rnv×nu maps actuator torques τ ∈ Rnu into generalized coordinates, and λ ∈ Rnc denotes the stacked contact-force coordinates acting through the contact Jacobian Jc: Q → Rnc×nv. Here, nc is the total number of scalar contact-force coordinates associated with all active contacts. B. Differentiable Contact Dynamics Rigid-body dynamics simulators compute contact forces λ and advance the system dynamics (1) with a variety of methods, including compliant models, complementarity problems, convex optimization, and more. Most simulators provide a discrete-time forward map xi+1 = f(xi, ui), (2) where xi and ui are the state and actuator command at the ith simulation time step. A selected actuator interface maps ui to the joint torque τi applied in (1), as detailed in Sec. III- A. Depending on the simulator, this map may also capture sticking and sliding contacts, impacts, joint-limit activation, and other constraints within a single discrete transition. We require that these forward dynamics are differentiable, that is, the partial derivatives ∂f ∂x, ∂f ∂u (3) are available. In this work, we use, which leverages a convex differentiable contact formulation to provide these gradients via finite differences. However, our framework is compatible with any differentiable simulator. III. TRAJECTORY OPTIMIZATION Our goal is to synthesize dynamically feasible wholebody trajectories that track a desired reference. Importantly, contact is not modeled explicitly in the optimization problem: no contact schedule or complementarity constraints are prescribed. Instead, contact behavior is resolved implicitly through the simulator dynamics (2). The tracking terms are defined relative to a reference trajectory Xref:= (xref 0,..., xref N ) that need not satisfy the whole-body dynamics (1). The reference may come from retargeted human motion-capture data, animation data, or a reduced-order model (ROM), whose trajectories are dynamically consistent only within the reduced representation. Fig. 2: Proposed multi-shooting trajectory optimization. A. Direct Simulation-based Multiple Shooting (DSMS) We employ direct multiple shooting to transcribe the trajectory optimization problem into a finite-dimensional nonlinear program (NLP). This transcription divides the horizon into N intervals, treats the shooting-node states as decision variables, and enforces continuity between independently integrated intervals through defect constraints. Shorter rollouts reduce long-horizon sensitivity and improve convergence, which is particularly valuable for highly dynamic, underactuated motions whose open-loop behavior is sensitive to early control decisions. We discretize the horizon [0, T] into N shooting intervals on the uniform grid tk:= k ∆t, k = 0,..., N, ∆t:= T/N. Let X:= (x0,..., xN) collect the state variables at the shooting nodes and let U:= (ξ1,..., ξM) collect M control points, with ξj ∈ Rnu. These control points parameterize the time-varying command signal through the map s: [0, T] × RMnu → Rnu, defined by u(t):= s(t, U) = M � j=1 βj(t)ξj. (4) Here, {βj}M j=1 are prescribed basis functions, such as zeroorder hold or piecewise linear. The actuator command u(t) is either a joint torque or a desired joint position tracked by a low-level PD controller,1 and uk:= u(tk) at node k. Using shooting-node states X and spline control points U, we transcribe the optimal control problem via direct multiple shooting as an NLP: min X,U J(X, U) (5a) s.t. xk+1 = F(xk, uk), k = 0,..., N − 1, (5b) g(xk, uk) ≤ 0, (5c) h(xk, uk) = 0. (5d) Here, the objective (5a) encodes tracking and regularization, and (5c) and (5d) collect inequality and equality constraints, such as path limits, boundary conditions, or task constraints. The flow map F in (5b) integrates (2) from xk under u(t) during [tk, tk+1), with the defect enforcing continuity between shooting intervals, as illustrated in Fig. 2. Fine simulator steps resolve stiff contact dynamics, while state variables only at the coarser shooting nodes keep the NLP small. Because the simulator directly defines the flow between shooting nodes, we refer to this formulation as direct simulation-based multiple shooting (DSMS). B. Cost Function The cost J(X, U) in (5a) is a weighted sum of state and body tracking, together with input regularizers penalizing torque effort and command rate. With state error ek:= xk ⊖ xref k, the state tracking term2 penalizes the tangent space deviation from the reference, ℓx(xk, k) = e⊤ k Qx ek, (6) with diagonal Qx ⪰ 0 weighting the configuration and velocity errors. In the style of the motion tracking objectives used in [2],, we track the pose and twist of a set of key bodies B, such as the feet, hands, and pelvis. The terminal state and body tracking terms retain the same form but with their weights scaled by γ > 1: ℓf x(xN) = γ ℓx(xN, N), (9a) ℓf y(xN) = γ ℓy(xN, N). (9b) Because the state and body errors are defined in different spaces—a generalized state space and a body-output space— the two terms are complementary: body tracking enforces task-relevant motion, while state tracking resolves kinematic redundancy and regularizes the whole-body posture. We regularize actuation with two terms. The first penalizes torque effort on the realized torque τk, ℓτ(xk, uk) = τ ⊤ k Rτ τk, (10) with diagonal Rτ ⪰ 0. C. Receding Horizon Control Full-horizon trajectory optimization solves the complete reference trajectory from a fixed initial state in a single solve. For highly dynamic humanoid motions, such as backflips and side rolls (Fig. 5), we instead apply (5) in a receding-horizon fashion. Full-horizon solves converge less reliably for such long, highly dynamic motions, whereas short replanning windows remain tractable and still yield a dynamically feasible rollout. Each solve spans a moving reference window of H intervals and duration TH = H∆t, shorter than the full trajectory. At the j-th replanning time ¯tj, we initialize the horizon from the current simulated state and shift the reference accordingly: x0 = x(¯tj), xref k = xref(¯tj + k∆t), (13) for k = 0,..., H. We then solve the corresponding H- interval horizon instance of (5), execute the first ∆trhc seconds of the optimized command, advance the simulator, and repeat with the shifted window. Concatenating the executed segments produces a long rollout whose transitions are generated directly by the simulator and therefore satisfy (1) by construction, rather than only up to the defect tolerance in (5b). D. Gait Synthesis To demonstrate that the proposed optimization can enforce constraints while preserving dynamic feasibility, we synthesize libraries of periodic walking, jogging, and crawling gaits from human motion-capture data, where each entry realizes a prescribed average base twist c:= (vx, vy, ωz) ∈ R3. Notably, crawling involves frequent contacts with the hands, elbows, knees, and feet, including sliding contacts. For each gait, forward, backward, and turning references, together with a static, zero-twist idle reference (standing or prone), tile the command space. Starting from a nearly periodic gait reference with period P, we solve the NLP (5) over a single gait cycle, using the equality constraints (5d) to enforce limit cycle closure. To formulate these constraints, we split the shooting-node state as xk = (zk, wk) ∈ Z × W. The first component is the planar base pose, zk:= � pxy k, ψk � ∈ Z, (14) containing the base horizontal position pxy k and heading ψk, with Z ∼= SE(2). The second component is the remaining state, wk:= � pz k, θk, qjnt k, vk � ∈ W, (15) containing the base height pz k, yaw-invariant tilt θk, joint positions qjnt k, and generalized velocities vk. The planar pose advances by the commanded displacement, zN = z0 ⊕ ∆z(c, P),3 which enforces a prescribed average base twist c. The remaining state satisfies w0 = wN, returning the height, tilt, joints, and velocities to their initial values and enforcing periodicity. Together, these constraints yield the limit cycle shown in Fig. 3a. Because closure determines the cycle only up to a planar rigid transformation, the tracking costs (6) and (8) anchor it to the gait reference, fully determining the remaining degrees of freedom. In addition to the cost (12), we add a no-slip term that penalizes the horizontal velocity of each contact link while it is planted. Because this term is a soft penalty rather than a hard constraint, it discourages unnecessary slipping while permitting the sliding contacts required by crawling, without excluding dynamically feasible solutions. Repeating this procedure for a range of commanded twists yields a library of command–gait pairs, in which each gait trajectory Xgait i is dynamically feasible under its corresponding command ci: L = {(ci, Xgait i )}Ngait i=1. Motion Imitation Following the motion-imitation framework of, we train RL policies to reproduce the generated reference motions. Given a reference trajectory from Sec. III-C, the policy learns to reproduce it using per-frame body pose and twist rewards, reference-state initialization, and adaptive frame sampling. Simulation deployment then measures how readily and accurately each reference can be learned and reproduced: a policy is trained on each reference and evaluated by how reliably and accurately it reproduces the motion during simulation rollouts. Sec. V-D uses these results to compare dynamic fidelity and retargeting methods. B. Locomotion Controller We train a single command-conditioned RL policy to track the gait library L. Given a commanded twist c, the nearest library trajectory provides the imitation target, allowing the discrete library to serve as a continuous velocity-command interface, as shown in Fig. 3b. We use an asymmetric actor-critic with a reference-free actor that observes signals available at deployment: oact = �ˆg, ωbase, qjnt, vjnt, aprev, c, sin(ϕ), cos(ϕ) �. (17) These comprise projected gravity ˆg, base angular velocity ωbase, joint positions and velocities qjnt, vjnt, previous action aprev, commanded twist c, and a sinusoidal encoding of the gait phase ϕ. During training, the critic additionally observes the base linear velocity, key-body poses (pB, qB), and gait reference: ocrit = � oact, vbase, pB, qB, xgait(c, ϕ) �. (18) Here, xgait(c, ϕ) is the reference state for command c at phase ϕ. The actor therefore requires only proprioception, command, and phase at inference. The action a specifies joint-position offsets applied through a PD controller. We use the gait’s idle posture (standing or prone) as the nominal pose, so zero action is valid and the policy learns only residual corrections. The reward consists of gait tracking, command tracking, and regularization: r = rgait + rtwist + rreg. (19) Following, rgait tracks key-body poses and velocities, together with the anchor position and orientation. The anchor target is propagated egocentrically by the reference anchor velocity and re-based at each command change to preserve translation and turning across gait cycles. Finally, rtwist tracks the commanded base twist, while rreg penalizes undesirable behavior such as jerky actions or unsafe contacts. All trajectories in L share period P, so a phase clock ϕ indexes the current imitation target. During an episode, resampling c selects the nearest gait without resetting the phase or robot state, while c = 0 selects the idle reference. At each switch, we blend the outgoing and incoming references at the shared phase while updating the command immediately, enabling smooth transitions. V. RESULTS A. Implementation Details We solve (5) with the interior-point solver via cyipopt, supplying the cost, constraints, and their first derivatives. IPOPT forms the NLP Lagrangian internally and factorizes each sparse KKT system with HSL ma57, exploiting the block-sparse multiple-shooting Jacobian. Since MuJoCo does not provide the second-order derivatives of (2) required by the Lagrangian Hessian,4 we use IPOPT’s limited-memory (L-BFGS) Hessian approximation built from the first-order derivatives (3). This approximation performs surprisingly well despite the stiff contact dynamics and abrupt curvature changes at contact events. We train RL policies for the Unitree G1 in mjlab with reference clips from the BONES-SEED human motion dataset.5 Policies are optimized with PPO via rsl rl, using (512, 256, 128) actor and critic MLPs. Simulated dynamics run at 200 Hz and the policy at 50 Hz, with 10 second episodes. For sim-to-real transfer, we randomize base pushes, center-of-mass offsets, joint-encoder biases, and contact friction. B. Hardware Deployment We first deploy a motion imitation policy trained to reproduce a 180◦ jump-turn reference from a single rigid-body (SRB) trajectory. The controller executes this highly dynamic maneuver by rotating the robot by approximately 180◦ during the jump and recovering to a stable landing (Fig. 1). We next deploy the RL locomotion controllers (Sec. IV- B) for walking, jogging, and crawling, steered in real time through commanded twists. Qualitative Capability Comparison To augment our discussion of retargeting and trajectory optimization approaches and situate DSMS among similar approaches, we present Table V. Here, whole-body dynamic feasibility refers to a trajectory satisfying (1), while arbitrary constraints refers to a method’s ability to enforce constraints of the form of (5c) and (5d). Although all four methods provide kinematic feasibility, they differ substantially in the physical and constrainthandling ability. OmniRetarget achieves excellent kinematic retargeting and often produces visually plausible trajectories, but it sacrifices dynamic feasibility for kinematic accuracy. SPARK shares this limitation, and although it can incorporate arbitrary constraints, it is not contact-implicit: it relies on holonomic constraints that require accurate contact detection for the solver to function. DynaRetarget instead samples rollouts to incorporate dynamics and handle contact implicitly; however, it is not able to accommodate arbitrary constraints. DSMS combines whole-body dynamic feasibility with a contact-implicit formulation, enabling contact-rich motions such as rolling and crawling without extensive tuning. It also supports arbitrary equality and inequality constraints. Our ablations further show that better-modeled trajectories yield better downstream tracking controllers, underscoring the importance of this approach. VI. CONCLUSION We presented a contact-implicit multi-shooting framework for transforming kinematically feasible references into dynamically feasible whole-body humanoid motions. By using a differentiable simulator as the transition model, the framework accounts for contact, friction, impacts, selfcollision, and actuation limits without requiring a prescribed contact sequence or manual constraint setup. The resulting reference trajectories improve downstream RL convergence and tracking performance while enabling contact-rich and dynamic behaviors such as walking, jogging, crawling, jumping, backflip, and side-rolling. Future work will investigate alternative differentiable simulators and sampling-based optimization methods, automatic discovery of contact-rich behaviors, robot–object interaction, and extension to additional robot morphologies.

papers.title: Sim-to-real transfer of active suspension control using deep reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: We explore sim-to-real transfer of deep reinforcement learning controllers for a heavy vehicle with active suspensions designed for traversing rough terrain. While related research primarily focuses on lightweight robots with electric motors and fast actuation, this study uses a forestry vehicle with a complex hydraulic driveline and slow actuation. We simulate the vehicle using multibody dynamics and apply system identification to find an appropriate set of simulation parameters. We then train policies in simulation using various techniques to mitigate the sim-to-real gap, including domain randomization, action delays, and a reward penalty to encourage smooth control. In reality, the policies trained with action delays and a penalty for erratic actions perform nearly at the same level as in simulation. In experiments on level ground, the motion trajectories closely overlap when turning to either side, as well as in a route tracking scenario. When faced with a ramp that requires active use of the suspensions, the simulated and real motions are in close alignment. This shows that the actuator model together with system identification yields a sufficiently accurate model of the actuators. We observe that policies trained without the additional action penalty exhibit fast switching or bang-bang control. These present smooth motions and high performance in simulation but transfer poorly to reality. We find that policies make marginal use of the local height map for perception, showing no indications of predictive planning. However, the strong transfer capabilities entail that further development concerning perception and performance can be largely confined to simulation.
papers.full_text: We explore sim-to-real transfer of deep reinforcement learning controllers for a heavy vehicle with active suspensions designed for traversing rough terrain. While related research primarily focuses on lightweight robots with electric motors and fast actuation, this study uses a forestry vehicle with a complex hydraulic driveline and slow actuation. We simulate the vehicle using multibody dynamics and apply system identification to find an appropriate set of simulation parameters. We then train policies in simulation using various techniques to mitigate the sim-to-real gap, including domain randomization, action delays, and a reward penalty to encourage smooth control. In reality, the policies trained with action delays and a penalty for erratic actions perform nearly at the same level as in simulation. In experiments on level ground, the motion trajectories closely overlap when turning to either side, as well as in a route tracking scenario. When faced with a ramp that requires active use of the suspensions, the simulated and real motions are in close alignment. This shows that the actuator model together with system identification yields a sufficiently accurate model of the actuators. We observe that policies trained without the additional action penalty exhibit fast switching or bang-bang control.
