(a) In the general case, the two safe regions partially overlap, and their intersection defines the feasible policy region satisfying both constraints. (b) When ¯D ≤ (1 − γ)¯c, the state-wise-cost safe region is contained within the cumulative-cost safe region, such that satisfying the state-wise constraint also guarantees the cumulative constraint. The first inequality follows from the state-wise cost increment construction in �t k=0 D(ˆsk, ak) = Mt+1 = max0≤k≤t c(ˆsk, ak), since the accumulated increments correspond to the maximum state-wise cost along the trajectory and therefore upper-bound the safety cost at every individual time step. The second inequality follows from the transformed state-wise constraint, while the equality follows from the geometric-series identity. Consequently, any policy satisfying the state-wise safety constraint also satisfies the cumulative cost constraint, which implies Πstate ⊆ Πcum. Therefore, under ¯D ≤ (1 − γ)¯c, the joint feasible region reduces to Πstate, as illustrated in Fig. 1(b). In the general case where this sufficient condition does not hold, such a containment relationship is not guaranteed, and the two feasible regions may only partially overlap, as shown in Fig. 1(a). MDPO therefore performs the joint projection toward their intersection to simultaneously account for both safety requirements. C. Practical Policy Optimization To implement the two-stage optimization described above, MDPO maintains a reward critic VR, a cumulative-cost critic VC, and a state-wise cost increment critic VD. Given the augmented observation ˆs = (st, Mt), the corresponding temporal-difference residuals are δR t = rt + γVR(ˆst+1) − VR(ˆst), δC t = ct + γVC(ˆst+1) − VC(ˆst), δD t = Dt + γVD(ˆst+1) − VD(ˆst). (19) The reward, cumulative-cost, and state-wise cost increment advantages are estimated using generalized advantage estimation (GAE), ˆAX t = �T −t−1 l=0 (γλGAE)l δX t+l, X ∈ {R, C, D}, where λGAE denotes the GAE trace parameter. The same λGAE is used for all three advantage estimators, whereas the contributions of the cumulative and state-wise safety constraints are independently regulated in the subsequent projection stage. Before performing the joint projection, MDPO estimates the current safety levels from completed trajectories. For cumulative safety, we use the mean episode cost ˆCk = Nk �Nk e=1 �Te−1 t=0 c(e) t, where Nk is the number of completed episodes at iteration k. For state-wise safety, the maximum instantaneous cost is first recorded for each episode, and a high quantile across the completed trajectories is used ˆDk = Qq �� maxt c(e) t �Nk e=1 �, where Qq denotes the q-quantile. We use q = 0.95 in our implementation, making the statewise safety estimate more sensitive to high-risk trajectories rather than allowing severe violations to be diluted by averaging. To reduce fluctuations induced by finite rollout samples, the two safety statistics are independently smoothed using exponential moving averages. Their normalized deviations from the corresponding safety targets are then computed as: vC = clip � ˆCk − bC bC, −1, 1 �, vD = clip � ˆDk − bD bD, −1, 1 �, (20) where bC = ρC¯c is a conservative cumulative-cost target with 0 < ρC < 1, and bD = ¯D is the state-wise target. In our implementation, ρC = 0.9. MDPO maintains two independent safety coefficients zC and zD, which are updated according to their respective constraint deviations: zC←Π[0,zmax C ](zC +ηChkvC),zD←Π[0,zmax D ](zD+ηDhkvD), (21) where ηC and ηD are independent adaptation rates, hk ∈ [0, 1] denotes the gradually activated constraint strength, and Π projects the coefficients onto their predefined ranges. Hence, when a safety statistic exceeds its target, the corresponding coefficient increases and imposes a stronger correction; when sufficient safety margin is available, the coefficient is gradually released. In practice, MDPO further incorporates the recent variation trend of each safety statistic into the effective coefficients. Specifically, a rapidly increasing cumulative or statewise safety risk strengthens its corresponding correction even before a severe violation is observed. The effective coefficients are additionally attenuated when a sufficiently large safety margin is available, avoiding unnecessary performance degradation. We denote the resulting coefficients used in the joint projection by: ωC = hkhCzC, ωD = hkhDzD, (22) where hC and hD modulate the correction strength according to the available safety margin. Importantly, ωC and ωD are independently adapted according to different safety statistics rather than sharing a common weighting coefficient. Using these adaptive safety coefficients, the second-stage joint projection is practically implemented as Eq. (15). Fig. 2. Performance comparison of MDPO with LAG, P3O, and CRPO on five dexterous manipulation tasks in ReDMan. From top to bottom, the rows correspond to Joint, Finger, Armjoint, Armfinger, and Grasp, while the columns report success rate, cost of episode, cost rate, and reward of episode, respectively. The solid curves denote the mean performance over three random seeds, the shaded regions indicate the corresponding standard deviation, and the black dashed lines represent the cumulative cost limits. TABLE I THE HYPER-PARAMETERS OF THE MDPO ALGORITHM MODEL. Hyper-parameters Setting Hyper-parameters Setting Discount factor γ 0.998 GAE trace parameter λGAE 0.95 Clipping coefficient ϵ 0.2 Projection clipping coefficient ϵP 0.2 Stage-2 KL coefficient κ0 0.75 State-wise risk quantile q 0.95 Initial cumulative coefficient z0 C 1e-4 Initial state-wise coefficient z0 D 1e-5 Cumulative adaptation rate ηC 3e-3 State-wise adaptation rate ηD 6e-5 Cumulative upper bound zmax C 0.5 State-wise upper bound zmax D 0.02 V. EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION In this section, we conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of MDPO in multi-constraint safe A. Experimental Setup Tasks. We evaluate MDPO on the benchmark, which provides standardized safety-constrained RL environments for dexterous manipulation. Five representative tasks are considered in our experiments, including Joint, Finger, Armjoint, Armfinger, and Grasp. These tasks cover different dexterous manipulation scenarios involving hand joints, fingers, coordinated arm-hand control, and object interaction. The original ReDMan environments characterize safety violations mainly using binary cost signals, where the cost changes abruptly between safe and unsafe states. To provide a denser safety signal for policy optimization and better reflect the severity of safety violations, we modify the original cost formulation into a continuous cost function while preserving the corresponding safety semantics of each task. The resulting continuous cost ct is used to construct both the cumulative and state-wise safety requirements. The running maximum cost Mt is incorporated into the observation, and the state-wise cost increment Dt is constructed to provide a tractable optimization signal for state-wise safety. For all tasks, we set the cumulative cost threshold ¯c = 35 and and state-wise cost threshold ¯D = 1. Baselines. We compare MDPO with three representative constrained RL methods, including LAG, P3O, and CRPO. Since these methods are originally designed mainly for conventional constrained RL settings, we adapt all of them to the same multi-constraint formulation considered in this work, such that both the cumulative cost constraint and the state-wise cost constraint are explicitly incorporated during policy optimization. Specifically, the multi-constraint LAG baseline introduces independent adaptive multipliers for the cumulative and state-wise safety constraints; P3O is extended by introducing separate penalty terms for the two safety objectives; and CRPO is adapted to account for both constraints when determining whether to optimize task performance or perform safety-oriented policy updates. These adaptations ensure that all baselines operate under the same cumulative and state-wise safety requirements as MDPO. All methods are trained using the same environment interaction budget and evaluated under identical task settings for a fair comparison. Implementation Details. The hyperparameters involved in the practical implementation of MDPO are summarized in Table I. The same settings are used across all tasks. B. Comparison Experiments Fig. 2 compares MDPO with the multi-constraint baselines LAG, P3O, and CRPO on five dexterous manipulation tasks. Overall, MDPO achieves a favorable balance between task performance and safety. Across the evaluated tasks, it reaches competitive or higher success rates and episode rewards while maintaining relatively low cumulative costs and statewise violation rates, indicating that the proposed method can effectively coordinate manipulation objectives with heterogeneous safety requirements. From the task-performance perspective, MDPO exhibits faster and more stable convergence on most tasks. On relatively simpler tasks such as Joint and Finger, several baselines can eventually reach comparable final performance, but generally require more interactions or show larger fluctuations during training. The advantage of MDPO becomes more evident on ArmJoint, ArmFinger, and particularly Grasp, where stronger arm-hand coordination and contact-rich interactions make policy learning more challenging. From the safety perspective, MDPO generally keeps the episode cost below or close to the prescribed cumulative cost limit while simultaneously achieving low cost rates. In contrast, some baselines can satisfy the cumulativecost requirement but still exhibit notable state-wise violations, indicating that existing constrained RL methods remain insufficient for simultaneously handling heterogeneous safety requirements. This result highlights the advantage of MDPO in jointly regulating long-horizon cumulative risks and instantaneous state-wise safety violations during policy optimization. These results validate the proposed two-stage optimization framework. MDPO first obtains a performanceimproved intermediate policy and then jointly corrects cumulative and state-wise safety risks through adaptive projection. The independently adjusted safety coefficients allow the two constraints to contribute according to their corresponding risk levels, while KL regularization limits excessive deviation from the intermediate policy. Consequently, MDPO achieves more stable multi-constraint satisfaction without sacrificing dexterous manipulation performance. C. Ablation Experiments Fig. 3 presents the ablation results on the Joint and Finger tasks. We compare the full MDPO with two single-constraint Fig. 3. Ablation study of MDPO on the Joint and Finger tasks. MDPO Cumulative and MDPO State retain only the cumulative-cost and state-wise safety corrections, respectively. From top to bottom, the rows report success rate, cost of episode, cost rate, and reward of episode. variants: MDPO Cumulative, which retains the cumulativecost safety correction, and MDPO State, which retains the state-wise safety correction. The comparison is conducted using success rate, cost of episode, cost rate, and reward of episode to investigate the individual and complementary contributions of the two safety constraints. Compared with the full MDPO, MDPO Cumulative can effectively regulate the episode-level cumulative cost, but generally exhibits a higher state-wise cost rate. This indicates that satisfying the cumulative constraint alone does not necessarily prevent transient unsafe behaviors, since short-duration violations contribute a limited amount to the total episode cost. Explicitly incorporating the state-wise cost signal is therefore important for suppressing safety-critical behaviors at individual interaction steps. MDPO State effectively reduces state-wise violations, but its task-performance improvement is generally slower and less stable than that of the full MDPO. Relying only on the state-wise constraint does not explicitly regulate the accumulated safety cost over the entire trajectory, which can restrict the balance between longhorizon safety and manipulation performance. In contrast, MDPO jointly exploits cumulative cost and state-wise cost increment advantages, enabling the two safety signals to complement each other during policy projection. Overall, the ablation results demonstrate that neither cumulative nor statewise safety regulation alone is sufficient to achieve the best performance-safety trade-off. The cumulative constraint controls long-term accumulated violations, while the state-wise constraint suppresses instantaneous safety-critical behaviors. Fig. 4. Real-world deployment of MDPO on the Grasp task. Left: grasping execution on a Tianji robotic arm equipped with a WujiHand dexterous hand. Right: the corresponding Grasp task in simulation. By jointly incorporating both constraints with independently adapted correction strengths, MDPO achieves more stable safety satisfaction while preserving competitive dexterous manipulation performance. D. Real-world Deployment To further evaluate the practical applicability of MDPO, we deploy the learned grasping policy on a real-world robotic platform consisting of a Tianji robotic arm and a WujiHand dexterous hand. As illustrated in Fig. 4, we present the corresponding manipulation behaviors in both simulation and the physical environment. The task requires coordinated armhand control while maintaining stable object interaction and avoiding aggressive or potentially unsafe hand motions. The policy learned with MDPO can be transferred to the physical platform and successfully execute the grasping behavior while preserving stable and safety-aware manipulation. This result demonstrates the potential of MDPO for transferring multi-constraint dexterous manipulation policies from simulation to real robotic systems. VI. CONCLUSION In this work, we propose the Multi-constraint Dexterous Policy Optimization for safe dexterous manipulation under both cumulative and state-wise safety constraints. To handle the heterogeneous temporal characteristics of these constraints, we reformulate the state-wise requirement into a tractable trajectory-level objective through a statewise cost increment formulation. Based on this formulation, MDPO adopts a two-stage optimization framework that first improves task performance and then jointly projects the intermediate policy toward the feasible region defined by both safety constraints. The joint projection incorporates cumulative and state-wise safety signals with independently adapted correction coefficients while using KL regularization to preserve the manipulation capability of the intermediate policy. Finally, extensive experiments on ReDMan demonstrate that MDPO achieves a favorable balance between task performance and multi-constraint safety.
